why: Erbb2 is the mouse ortholog of human ERBB2 and encodes HER2 (ErbB2), a receptor tyrosine kinase of the ErbB/EGFR family. HER2 has no known direct ligand and signals through heterodimerization with other ErbB receptors, and has been associated with activation of downstream pathways including RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT.

ERBB2 amplification or overexpression has been associated with a subset of breast and gastric cancers, and HER2-directed antibodies, antibody–drug conjugates, and kinase inhibitors are used in HER2-positive disease; responses vary by tumor type and prior therapy. Mouse models expressing human ERBB2 have been used to study HER2 biology and HER2-targeted agents.
applications: Humanized ERBB2 models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate HER2-directed antibodies and antibody–drug conjugates in immunocompetent mice.
Transgenic and knock-in Erbb2 models have been used to study HER2-driven tumorigenesis in defined experimental settings.

why: Egfr is the mouse ortholog of human EGFR and encodes the epidermal growth factor receptor (HER1/ErbB1), a receptor tyrosine kinase activated by ligands including EGF and TGF-α. Ligand binding promotes receptor dimerization and signaling through pathways including RAS–MAPK and PI3K–AKT, which have been associated with cell proliferation and survival.

Activating EGFR mutations and overexpression have been associated with non-small cell lung cancer and other tumors, and EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors and antibodies are used in selected EGFR-driven cancers; resistance commonly emerges. Homozygous Egfr-null mice show strain-dependent lethality and epithelial defects.
applications: Humanized EGFR models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate EGFR-targeted antibodies and inhibitors.
Conditional and mutant Egfr models have been used to study EGFR signaling and EGFR-driven disease in defined experimental settings.

why: Cd47 is the mouse ortholog of human CD47 and encodes CD47 (integrin-associated protein), a widely expressed cell-surface protein. CD47 binds the myeloid receptor SIRPα and has been associated with a signal that limits macrophage phagocytosis, sometimes described as a ‘don’t-eat-me’ signal.

CD47 overexpression on tumor cells has been associated with evasion of macrophage clearance in some contexts, and CD47-SIRPα-targeted agents have been evaluated in cancer; reported clinical results have varied. Cd47-deficient mice are viable and show altered clearance of circulating cells.
applications: Humanized CD47 models, often combined with SIRPα humanization, have been used to evaluate CD47-SIRPα-targeted therapeutics and to support engraftment of human cells.
Cd47 knockout mice have been used to study macrophage regulation in defined experimental settings.

why: Tnfrsf17 is the mouse ortholog of human TNFRSF17 and encodes BCMA (B-cell maturation antigen, CD269), a TNF-receptor-superfamily member expressed mainly on plasma cells and late-stage B cells. BCMA binds the ligands BAFF and APRIL and has been associated with plasma-cell survival and antibody responses.

BCMA is expressed on malignant plasma cells in multiple myeloma, and BCMA-directed CAR T cells and bispecific antibodies are used in relapsed or refractory disease; responses vary and relapse can occur. Tnfrsf17-deficient mice are viable with reduced numbers of long-lived plasma cells.
applications: Humanized TNFRSF17 (BCMA) models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate BCMA-directed CAR T cells and bispecific antibodies in immunocompetent mice, including in combination settings.
Tnfrsf17 models have been used to study plasma-cell biology in defined experimental settings.

why: Glp1r is the mouse ortholog of human GLP1R and encodes the glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor, a class B G-protein-coupled receptor. GLP-1R signaling, primarily through Gs and cAMP, has been associated with glucose-dependent insulin secretion, slowed gastric emptying, and reduced food intake.

GLP-1 receptor agonists are used in type 2 diabetes and obesity, and the receptor is a target of several marketed and investigational agents. Glp1r-deficient mice are viable and show altered glucose tolerance and insulin secretion.
applications: Humanized GLP1R models, in which the human receptor replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate GLP-1-receptor-targeted peptides and small molecules in vivo.
Glp1r knockout and reporter models have been used to study incretin signaling and receptor distribution.

why: Il13 is the mouse ortholog of human IL13 and encodes interleukin-13, a type 2 cytokine produced mainly by T helper 2 cells and other immune cells. IL-13 signals through receptor complexes that include IL-4Rα and has been associated with promotion of IgE responses, mucus production, and tissue changes in type 2 inflammation.

IL-13, together with IL-4, is implicated in atopic dermatitis, asthma, and other allergic diseases, and IL-13-directed antibodies are in clinical use. Il13-deficient mice are viable and show impaired type 2 responses in disease models.
applications: Humanized IL13 models, often paired with humanized IL-13 or IL-4 receptor components, have been used to evaluate IL-13-targeted antibodies in defined experimental settings.
Il13 knockout mice have been used to study type 2 immunity and allergic inflammation.

why: C5 is the mouse ortholog of human C5 and encodes complement component C5, a protein of the terminal complement pathway. C5 is cleaved to generate the anaphylatoxin C5a and the fragment C5b, which initiates assembly of the membrane attack complex, and has been associated with inflammation and cell lysis.

The terminal complement pathway, including C5, is implicated in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and other conditions, and C5-directed antibodies are in clinical use. Mouse strains deficient in C5 activity show altered complement-dependent responses and susceptibility to certain challenges.
applications: Humanized C5 models, in which the human protein replaces the mouse counterpart, have been used to evaluate C5-targeted therapeutics in defined experimental settings.
C5 models have been used to study terminal complement activity.
